## Pharmacokinetics and Dosing
Beta-blockers block beta receptors. This lowers heart rate and blood pressure.
Some are beta-1 selective. They work on the heart. Examples: metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol.
Some are non-selective. They block beta-1 and beta-2. This can cause bronchoconstriction. Examples: propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol.
Some are mixed alpha/beta. They also block alpha-1, causing vasodilation. Examples: carvedilol, labetalol.
Bioavailability is how much drug reaches the blood. Metoprolol and atenolol are 50%. Propranolol is 30% due to high first-pass.
Half-life is how long the drug stays active. Metoprolol 3-7 h (ER 12 h), bisoprolol 10-12 h, carvedilol 7-10 h, nebivolol 12-20 h.
Renal excretion: atenolol, nadolol, sotalol need dose adjustment if CrCl <30 mL/min.
Typical adult doses: metoprolol tartrate 50-100 mg bid, ER 25-200 mg; atenolol 25-100 mg; bisoprolol 1.25-10 mg; carvedilol 3.125-25 mg bid; nebivolol 2.5-20 mg; propranolol 40-160 mg tid/qid (IR) or 80-160 mg LA; sotalol 80-160 mg bid.
Indications: hypertension, angina, post-MI, HFrEF (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol-ER, nebivolol), AF rate control, ventricular arrhythmia (sotalol), migraine (propranolol), essential tremor, glaucoma (topical timolol).
Key: Beta-blockers block beta receptors, lowering heart rate and blood pressure.
Key: Beta-1 selective: metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol.
Key: Non-selective: propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol.
Key: Mixed alpha/beta: carvedilol, labetalol.
Key: Bioavailability: metoprolol 50%, atenolol 50%, propranolol 30%.
Key: Half-life: metoprolol 3-7 h (ER 12 h), bisoprolol 10-12 h, carvedilol 7-10 h, nebivolol 12-20 h.

Q: Which drug has the lowest oral bioavailability? A: Propranolol. Propranolol has 30% bioavailability, the lowest.
Q: Which drug needs dose adjustment in renal impairment? A: Atenolol. Atenolol is renally excreted, so adjust if CrCl <30.
Q: Which drug is used for migraine prophylaxis? A: Propranolol. Propranolol is used for migraine prophylaxis.

## Clinical Indications and Contraindications
Beta-blockers work by blocking beta-adrenergic receptors. This lowers heart rate, contractility, and renin release.
There are three types. Beta-1 selective ones (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) mainly affect the heart. Non-selective ones (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) also block beta-2, which can cause bronchoconstriction. Mixed alpha/beta ones (carvedilol, labetalol) add vasodilation.
Main uses: high blood pressure, stable angina, after a heart attack, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) using bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol-ER, or nebivolol, rate control in atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmia prevention with sotalol, migraine prevention with propranolol, essential tremor, and glaucoma with topical timolol.
Typical adult doses (once daily unless noted): metoprolol tartrate 50–100 mg twice daily, ER 25–200 mg; atenolol 25–100 mg; bisoprolol 1.25–10 mg; carvedilol 3.125–25 mg twice daily; nebivolol 2.5–20 mg; propranolol 40–160 mg three or four times daily (IR) or 80–160 mg LA; sotalol 80–160 mg twice daily.
Avoid in asthma or COPD with reversible bronchospasm, especially non-selective. Also avoid in sinus bradycardia below 50 bpm, second or third degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome, cardiogenic shock, and decompensated heart failure (start only when euvolemic).
Use caution in severe peripheral arterial disease, pregnancy (avoid atenolol, prefer labetalol), and diabetes (can mask hypoglycemia; prefer beta-1 selective or nebivolol). CYP2D6 poor metabolizers have higher metoprolol and carvedilol levels.
Key interactions: increased bradycardia with digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem, ivabradine; increased hypotension with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics; NSAIDs reduce antihypertensive effect; CYP2D6 inhibitors like fluoxetine and paroxetine raise metoprolol.
Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, ECG, renal function, potassium, glucose, and lipids (non-selective raise triglycerides, lower HDL). Adverse effects: fatigue, cold extremities, sexual dysfunction, then bronchospasm, then hyperglycemia mask, depression (rare), heart block.
Do not stop suddenly—can cause rebound tachycardia, hypertension, ischemia. Taper over 1–2 weeks. In elderly, start low and go slow. In CKD, use renally cleared agents (atenolol, nadolol) with dose reduction. In heart failure, uptitrate to target doses: bisoprolol 10 mg, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, metoprolol-ER 200 mg.

Key: Contraindications: asthma, bradycardia, AV block, cardiogenic shock, decompensated HF
Key: Cautions: PAD, pregnancy, diabetes, CYP2D6 poor metabolizers
Key: Doses: typical adult doses for each agent
Key: Interactions: bradycardia, hypotension, NSAIDs, CYP2D6 inhibitors

## Drug Interactions, Monitoring, and Adverse Effects
Beta-blockers are not for everyone. Avoid them in asthma with reversible bronchospasm, slow heart rate under 50, heart block, cardiogenic shock, and decompensated heart failure unless the patient is euvolemic (normal fluid status).
In pregnancy, avoid atenolol because it can harm the baby; labetalol is preferred. In diabetes, beta-blockers can hide low blood sugar signs, so prefer beta-1 selective ones or nebivolol.
Some people are CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, so metoprolol and carvedilol levels rise. CYP2D6 inhibitors like fluoxetine and paroxetine also raise metoprolol.
Watch for drug interactions: digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem, ivabradine increase bradycardia. ACEi/ARB and diuretics increase hypotension. NSAIDs lower the antihypertensive effect.
Monitor HR, BP, ECG, renal function, potassium, glucose, and lipids. Non-selective beta-blockers raise triglycerides and lower HDL.
Adverse effects, from most to least common: fatigue, cold extremities, sexual dysfunction; then bronchospasm (non-selective); then masking hyperglycemia; then depression (rare); then heart block.
Stopping suddenly can cause rebound tachycardia, hypertension, and ischemia. Taper over 1–2 weeks.
In elderly, start low and go slow. In CKD, use renally cleared agents like atenolol or nadolol with dose reduction. In heart failure, uptitrate to target doses: bisoprolol 10 mg, carvedilol 25 mg bid, metoprolol-ER 200 mg.

Key: Monitoring: HR, BP, ECG, renal, K+, glucose, lipids.

Key: Withdrawal: taper over 1–2 weeks to avoid rebound.

In asthma or COPD with reversible bronchospasm, avoid non-selective beta-blockers. They can cause bronchospasm, which is a narrowing of the airways. Even a β1-selective agent can cause bronchospasm at high doses, so it is not first-line.
Other cautions: avoid in sinus bradycardia (heart rate <50 bpm), 2nd/3rd degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome, cardiogenic shock, and decompensated heart failure (start only when euvolemic). In severe peripheral arterial disease, there is a risk of ischemia.

Do not stop abruptly. Abrupt cessation causes rebound tachycardia, hypertension, and ischemia. Taper over 1–2 weeks.
